nameStory: The red-leaved rose gets its name from its distinctive purplish-red to blue-gray foliage that sets it apart from other roses. Unlike most roses that are known for their flowers, this species is prized by gardeners specifically for its colorful leaves that create a stunning backdrop in the landscape. The scientific name 'glauca' means 'blue-gray,' referring to the waxy, frosted appearance of the leaves.
description: Red-leaved rose is a graceful shrub rose that stands out for its unusual foliage rather than its flowers. This European native grows 4-6 feet tall and wide, with arching canes that create an elegant, fountain-like shape. The most striking feature is its blue-gray to purplish-red leaves that have a waxy, almost frosted appearance. Small pink flowers appear in early summer, followed by bright red rose hips in fall.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive blue-gray to purplish-red compound leaves with 5-7 leaflets that feel waxy and smooth to the touch, creating an almost frosted appearance unlike any other rose

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, single pink flowers about 1 inch across with 5 petals and prominent yellow centers, appearing in small clusters in early summer

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Arching, fountain-like shrub reaching 4-6 feet tall with smooth, reddish canes that have fewer thorns than most roses

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright orange-red rose hips that are oval-shaped and persist into winter, feeling firm and smooth when fresh

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young canes are distinctly reddish-purple and relatively smooth, with scattered small thorns rather than the dense prickles of many roses

habitat: Red-leaved rose is extremely rare in New England, found almost exclusively in cultivated settings like botanical gardens, arboreta, or specialty rose gardens. This mountain species from Europe prefers well-drained soils and cooler conditions, making it challenging to establish in New England's climate. When found, it's typically in protected locations with some afternoon shade.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge with their distinctive blue-gray color, often tinged with purple or red tones that intensify as they mature.
seasonality.summer: Small pink flowers bloom in early summer, while the unusual leaf color remains the main attraction throughout the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Bright orange-red rose hips ripen and the colorful foliage may develop additional purple tints before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Smooth reddish canes and persistent rose hips make identification possible, though the distinctive leaves are gone.

funFact: Red-leaved rose is so rare in New England that it has been observed only once in the entire region according to botanical records, making it one of the rarest roses you could possibly encounter in the wild!
confusionNotes: The distinctive blue-gray to purplish foliage makes this rose nearly impossible to confuse with any other rose species in New England. No other rose has this waxy, frosted leaf coloration - if you see these unusual colored leaves on a rose, you've found something very special.
contextualKnowledge: This rose is sometimes called Rosa rubrifolia in older gardening books, which was its former scientific name. While native to European mountains, it's primarily known in North America as an ornamental plant valued more for its foliage than its flowers, reversing the usual priority for roses.
compareHints: Unlike New England's native roses such as swamp rose or Carolina rose which have green leaves, red-leaved rose's blue-gray to purplish foliage is unmistakable. It also has smoother canes with fewer thorns compared to the heavily armed multiflora rose or rugosa rose. The small, simple pink flowers are much less showy than rugosa rose's large blooms or the clustered flowers of multiflora rose.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England roses, multiflora rose is unique for its enormous flower clusters (other roses have flowers in smaller groups or singly) and those telltale fringed stipules.
Rugosa rose stands apart from other New England roses with its unmistakable wrinkled leaves - no other rose species has this corrugated texture.

Among New England's wild roses, swamp rose is unique in its preference for wet habitats - while Carolina rose and Virginia rose stick to drier areas, and multiflora rose (an invasive) has much denser thorns and forms larger, more aggressive colonies.
Among New England's wild roses, Carolina rose is the champion spreader, forming low colonies while relatives like swamp rose grow taller and more upright.
Among New England's wild roses, Virginian rose stands out for its glossy leaflets (rugosa rose has wrinkled leaves) and typically 7-9 leaflets per leaf (most others have fewer).

Among New England's roses, Sherard's downy-rose stands out for its compact size and distinctly grayish, downy leaves - most other wild roses like swamp rose or Carolina rose have greener, smoother foliage.

Among New England's wild roses, smooth rose is unique for its nearly thornless stems – multiflora rose has curved thorns, rugosa rose has dense straight prickles, and swamp rose has scattered thorns along its stems.
Among New England's roses, dog-rose stands out for its large, curved thorns and smooth leaflets without fuzzy coating.
Memorial rose is unique among New England roses for its prostrate, ground-hugging growth habit - all other rose species in the region grow as upright shrubs.
Among New England's wild roses, shining rose is uniquely low-growing and has by far the glossiest leaves.
Unlike the common multiflora rose with its clusters of small white flowers, cinnamon rose has larger, solitary pink blooms.
Among New England's wild roses, prickly wild rose stands out for its extreme thorniness — it has far more prickles per inch than rugosa rose, swamp rose, or any of our other native roses.
Among New England's roses, sweet-brier is the only one with apple-scented leaves - this fragrance alone separates it from multiflora rose, rugosa rose, and native species.
Climbing prairie rose stands out from other New England roses primarily by its vigorous climbing habit with long, flexible canes.
